Speaker: L:
Text: This is Jessica Lancia.

Speaker: L:
Text: I am with the Samuel Proctor Oral History Project and we are interviewing today Mrs. Alethia Viola Brown and we are in the Hawthorne Library and it is August 10, 2011.

Speaker: L:
Text: So first of all, thank you so much for agreeing to do this interview today.

Speaker: L:
Text: Do you mind saying your whole name, spelling it, and what is your date of birth?

Speaker: B:
Text: My first name is A-L-E-T-H-I-A, Viola V-I-O-L-A, Brown, B-R-O-W-N.

Speaker: L:
Text: And when were you born?

Speaker: B:
Text: Seventh month, 28, '21

Speaker: L:
Text: March 28th?

Speaker: B:
Text: Seventh month.

Speaker: B:
Text: July 28th, '21.

Speaker: L:
Text: Okay, 1921.

Speaker: L:
Text: Great.

Speaker: L:
Text: And where were you born?

Speaker: B:
Text: Hawthorne.

Speaker: L:
Text: In Hawthorne.

Speaker: L:
Text: All right, so…

Speaker: B:
Text: The place is called Gordon Chapel where I was born, but, a lot of people wouldn’t know, but I well-rooted from Hawthorne.

Speaker: L:
Text: All right.

Speaker: L:
Text: And who were your parents?

Speaker: L:
Text: What were their names?

Speaker: B:
Text: Andrew and Susie McCone.

Speaker: L:
Text: McCowan?

Speaker: B:
Text: M-C-C-O-N-E.

Speaker: L:
Text: And were they from Hawthorne, as well?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: B:
Text: They were residents of Hawthorne.

Speaker: L:
Text: All right, and what about your grandparents?

Speaker: L:
Text: Do you remember them?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: B:
Text: My grandmother was born there also, in Hawthorne.

Speaker: B:
Text: And grandfather too.

Speaker: L:
Text: So, did you have any siblings?

Speaker: L:
Text: Brothers and sisters?

Speaker: B:
Text: Oh, you mean children or brothers and sisters?

Speaker: L:
Text: Did you have any brothers and sisters?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yes, it was nine of us.

Speaker: L:
Text: Wow.

Speaker: L:
Text: Was that considered a big family?

Speaker: B:
Text: A big family?

Speaker: B:
Text: Well, I would consider it being, yeah.

Speaker: B:
Text: It was nine boys and four girl.

Speaker: B:
Text: I meant to say it was five boys and four girls.

Speaker: L:
Text: Wow.

Speaker: L:
Text: So what was Hawthorne like when you were growing up?

Speaker: B:
Text: Well now, we didn’t grow up in Hawthorne.

Speaker: B:
Text: We grew up in Putnam County.

Speaker: B:
Text: And we moved to a building in Hawthorne.

Speaker: B:
Text: I build a home in Hawthorne.

Speaker: B:
Text: And we moved up after I finished high school.

Speaker: B:
Text: But we walked to Hawthorne to high school.

Speaker: B:
Text: We went to Gordon Chapel to elementary school through sixth grade and then we walked seventh grade through twelfth grade to Hawthorne from Gordon Chapel.

Speaker: B:
Text: And from Putnam Country to Alachua County.

Speaker: L:
Text: So that’s six miles.

Speaker: L:
Text: How long did that take you to walk?

Speaker: B:
Text: Oh, well, we would had to run a lot.

Speaker: B:
Text: We’d leave home maybe, I’d say around 7:30 sometime.

Speaker: B:
Text: We’d run and walk and run and we'd be late a few mornings.

Speaker: B:
Text: Most of the time we’d be on time.

Speaker: L:
Text: What time did you school start?

Speaker: B:
Text: What time is it over?

Speaker: B:
Text: Eight o’clock.

Speaker: L:
Text: Wow.

Speaker: L:
Text: So, you grew up near Hawthorne?

Speaker: L:
Text: Six miles away.

Speaker: B:
Text: Six miles east of Hawthorne.

Speaker: B:
Text: At Gordon Chapel.

Speaker: L:
Text: East.

Speaker: L:
Text: And what was it like growing up there?

Speaker: B:
Text: It was nice.

Speaker: B:
Text: We had a farm.

Speaker: B:
Text: We was on eight acres of land.

Speaker: B:
Text: We had a farm and planted out there.

Speaker: B:
Text: And you know, we grew our food and had our hogs, cows for milk and all.

Speaker: L:
Text: Wow.

Speaker: L:
Text: So your parents, they were farmers?

Speaker: B:
Text: They were what?

Speaker: L:
Text: Were they farmers?

Speaker: L:
Text: Your parents?

Speaker: B:
Text: Were they what?

Speaker: L:
Text: Farmers.

Speaker: L:
Text: Were they farmers?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, they would farm.

Speaker: B:
Text: They would farm.

Speaker: B:
Text: They had a garden 'specially if they planted in the fields.

Speaker: B:
Text: For the cows.

Speaker: L:
Text: And did they sell their produce or —?

Speaker: B:
Text: No.

Speaker: B:
Text: We just fed the cows.

Speaker: L:
Text: It was for you?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, planting it for the cows and for ourselves.

Speaker: L:
Text: So, when you were in school, what was your school like?

Speaker: B:
Text: What was it like?

Speaker: L:
Text: To be in school.

Speaker: B:
Text: It was, you know, elementary school was nice.

Speaker: B:
Text: It was quite nice, we had a nice teacher.

Speaker: B:
Text: You know, a lady from down in Putnam County.

Speaker: B:
Text: It was the kind we lived in.

Speaker: B:
Text: She was very good, but we had more than one teacher.

Speaker: B:
Text: It was about three teachers, different teachers there doing my years there.

Speaker: B:
Text: But mostly, this lady I’m talking about, the Johnson lady.

Speaker: B:
Text: This the main teacher we had.

Speaker: L:
Text: And she taught you all the subjects?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, she taught everybody, all the classes.

Speaker: B:
Text: First through seventh.

Speaker: B:
Text: Eighth grade, what was eighth grade?

Speaker: B:
Text: I think it was first through eighth grade, she taught by herself.

Speaker: B:
Text: No other teachers, just one teacher.

Speaker: L:
Text: And how many students were in your school?

Speaker: B:
Text: It must have been around, maybe thirty.

Speaker: B:
Text: Around thirty.

Speaker: L:
Text: Was it a one building?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, just one building.

Speaker: L:
Text: And did it have more than one --

Speaker: B:
Text: And you know different classes would be on, one would be here and one be over here.

Speaker: B:
Text: Different places, you know, in the school.

Speaker: L:
Text: So, what did you enjoy about school?

Speaker: B:
Text: I enjoyed the lesson, I think.

Speaker: B:
Text: Better than I did anything else.

Speaker: B:
Text: I wanted to know, well, I would do a lot of reading so I wouldn’t miss out on anything, so I’d know when I got to school, I'd know what was going on and I could talk about it.

Speaker: B:
Text: I liked the feeling of knowing what was going on.

Speaker: B:
Text: I liked to talk.

Speaker: L:
Text: What about, what were your favorite subjects?

Speaker: B:
Text: I didn’t have no special subjects.

Speaker: B:
Text: I just loved all of it.

Speaker: B:
Text: I just loved school.

Speaker: B:
Text: I just loved school.

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, I liked spelling, arithmetic, and reading a lot.

Speaker: B:
Text: You know, up in the grades like, you could, you know, read the high books, you know, on something about the world business.

Speaker: L:
Text: So was it, who was in your school, were all of your brothers and sisters in the same school with you?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, those were able to go at that time, ages ago, at that time -- see I was the third child, there was three of us at one time.

Speaker: B:
Text: One and then one time, you know, as you got six years old, you know, they could go, see, and my older brother was ahead of us, then the next one was ahead, and then myself.

Speaker: B:
Text: And it just kept on that way, everyone was a grade ahead of each other.

Speaker: L:
Text: So there was one year between all of the —

Speaker: B:
Text: All of us.

Speaker: L:
Text: All of you.

Speaker: L:
Text: So, when it was time for the crops to be harvested or the cows to be milked, did you help with that or did your parents do all of that work?

Speaker: B:
Text: When it was soon as we got old enough to do it so, we started doing it.

Speaker: B:
Text: My daddy didn't never milk 'em but my mother would milk but, she could stop after we got large enough, you know, to milk, we done so ourselves.

Speaker: L:
Text: How old were you when you started milking the cows?

Speaker: B:
Text: Beg pardon?

Speaker: L:
Text: How old were you when you started milking the cows?

Speaker: B:
Text: I must have been around seven when I started.

Speaker: L:
Text: And then so would you milk the cows and then go to school?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: B:
Text: We started milking the cow and then turned the cows out and the calves would stay in all day.

Speaker: B:
Text: And we'd go to school.

Speaker: B:
Text: My daddy was working, you know, he’d go to work early in the morning at the kaolin mine.

Speaker: L:
Text: At the mine?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah.

Speaker: B:
Text: The kaolin mine.

Speaker: L:
Text: So he would go to work at the mine and your mother would stay at the farm.

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah.

Speaker: L:
Text: And your kids, all of the kids would go.

Speaker: L:
Text: So your mother really did most of the farming?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, yeah.

Speaker: B:
Text: I mean he would hire people to come in and plant things, you know -- 'course, we didn’t have a horse.

Speaker: B:
Text: We didn’t keep a horse because it was something we couldn’t keep up with, wouldn't my daddy keep up with it.

Speaker: B:
Text: So, he was working at the kaolin mine.

Speaker: B:
Text: And he would just get somebody come in and plant.

Speaker: L:
Text: Did he ever tell you stories about what it was like to work in the mine?

Speaker: B:
Text: Well, we were kind of small then and we didn’t pay much attention to that, you know, as to how they would do what they do there.

Speaker: B:
Text: Kaolin mine down in Johnson, they called it.

Speaker: B:
Text: He didn’t have to go far, you know -- well, he went a long ways too, but he walked.

Speaker: B:
Text: He could walk where he was going.

Speaker: B:
Text: From Putnam -- Alachua County to Putnam County.

Speaker: L:
Text: So had they bought the land or was the land given to them?

Speaker: B:
Text: Who?

Speaker: B:
Text: My daddy?

Speaker: L:
Text: Yeah, your parents.

Speaker: L:
Text: Yeah.

Speaker: B:
Text: He bought it.

Speaker: B:
Text: He must have because they had it when his mother was living.

Speaker: B:
Text: His mother lived with him, you know, 'fore he married me.

Speaker: L:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: L:
Text: So it was his land, and maybe his parent’s land before that.

Speaker: L:
Text: And then your mother came and lived with him?

Speaker: B:
Text: That’s right.

Speaker: L:
Text: And where was she from?

Speaker: B:
Text: She was from Hawthorne.

Speaker: B:
Text: She was there out from Hawthorne.

Speaker: B:
Text: You know.

Speaker: L:
Text: Did they ever tell you a story about how they met?

Speaker: B:
Text: I’m just wondering.

Speaker: B:
Text: Anyway, he married her very young, you know.

Speaker: L:
Text: Very young.

Speaker: B:
Text: And then moved with her.

Speaker: B:
Text: And married her in Palatka, and 'course they didn’t bother -- she must've been old enough for them not to bother.

Speaker: B:
Text: But, she was young.

Speaker: L:
Text: And what was she like?

Speaker: B:
Text: Quiet, you know.

Speaker: B:
Text: Very workable.

Speaker: B:
Text: She loved gardening.

Speaker: B:
Text: And milked the cows, you know, and she’d help, you know, she a good housekeeper.

Speaker: L:
Text: She worked hard?

Speaker: B:
Text: Huh?

Speaker: L:
Text: She worked hard.

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, she worked hard.

Speaker: L:
Text: And what was your dad like?

Speaker: B:
Text: He was the same way.

Speaker: B:
Text: Course, he walked to work a lot of time.

Speaker: B:
Text: He didn’t get a ride.

Speaker: B:
Text: He’d get up early enough to walk to his job.

Speaker: L:
Text: Now when you went to school, was it a segregated school?

Speaker: L:
Text: Were there any White children in your school?

Speaker: B:
Text: No.

Speaker: B:
Text: It was years before I went to school.

Speaker: B:
Text: I don’t remember ever going, you know, with White children, until I, you know, finished high school and went to college.

Speaker: L:
Text: Right, so you were in a segregated, I mean everything was segregated.

Speaker: B:
Text: Everything was segregated, everything was segregated.

Speaker: L:
Text: So when you went to high school, here, in Hawthorne, what was the difference between -- do you remember the difference between the high school here and the middle school where you were closer to?

Speaker: B:
Text: No, they were all the same 'cause I don’t ever remember them changing, you know, bringing in Whites or anything, mixing them, during the time that I was in school.

Speaker: L:
Text: Because you were, how old were, what year did you graduate from high school, do you remember?

Speaker: B:
Text: I think it was 1940.

Speaker: L:
Text: Oh yeah, way before, way before.

Speaker: L:
Text: So 1940, that was around World War II.

Speaker: L:
Text: Just happened.

Speaker: B:
Text: See what happened was nobody was going to war, nobody went to war.

Speaker: B:
Text: They didn’t have anybody old enough, you know, to go to war.

Speaker: B:
Text: So I don’t remember anyone, but I had brothers under me who went to war.

Speaker: B:
Text: No one left to go to war.

Speaker: L:
Text: So you must have been nineteen, eighteen, nineteen years old --

Speaker: B:
Text: When I finished high school?

Speaker: L:
Text: Yeah.

Speaker: B:
Text: I was eighteen when I finished high school.

Speaker: L:
Text: And your little brother --

Speaker: B:
Text: But we had to walk to Hawthorne then, 'cause see, we couldn’t go in Putnam County because we only went to sixth grade.

Speaker: B:
Text: After sixth grade, we walked to Hawthorne, to high school.

Speaker: B:
Text: That’s where we had to do that.

Speaker: L:
Text: So what did you do after high school?

Speaker: B:
Text: Went to college.

Speaker: B:
Text: Went to Florida A&M, yep.

Speaker: L:
Text: And how was that?

Speaker: B:
Text: That was good, I done good.

Speaker: B:
Text: But I learned, I mean, I didn’t have taught one year because they were short of teachers.

Speaker: B:
Text: I taught one year out in Marianna.

Speaker: B:
Text: But I wanted to do something else, they were building ships, welding and all.

Speaker: B:
Text: And that’s what I started building.

Speaker: B:
Text: I took welding.

Speaker: B:
Text: Welding, that’s where I build a home in Hawthorne.

Speaker: L:
Text: So when you were in college though, you said that you played basketball?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah.

Speaker: L:
Text: Can you tell me about that?

Speaker: B:
Text: I done good -- I could play good.

Speaker: B:
Text: I did have a lot of my brothers to, you know, at home, and it made me a little rough.

Speaker: B:
Text: I could move on the field once I learned play basketball.

Speaker: B:
Text: I could play now.

Speaker: B:
Text: I’d do all that jumping and everything you need to do.

Speaker: B:
Text: I was very active and I liked playing it very much.

Speaker: B:
Text: We had a good team.

Speaker: L:
Text: How did you decide to join the team?

Speaker: B:
Text: I just liked seeing them play and wanted to play.

Speaker: L:
Text: And they had an all-ladies basketball team?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, all ladies.

Speaker: B:
Text: And then they had all men basketball -- boys and girls played.

Speaker: B:
Text: So both teams would go wherever they're going -- the boys played and the girls play.

Speaker: L:
Text: What schools did you play?

Speaker: B:
Text: We played --

Speaker: U:
Text: Hastings.

Speaker: B:
Text: Oh, a lot of schools we played now --

Speaker: U:
Text: Alachua

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, Alachua, High Springs, and Gainesville, and Ocala, Palatka.

Speaker: B:
Text: We played most of the schools around there.

Speaker: L:
Text: That was in high school?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah.

Speaker: L:
Text: So you were on the basketball team in high school and in college?

Speaker: B:
Text: And in college.

Speaker: B:
Text: I didn’t play one year in college.

Speaker: L:
Text: You didn’t play one year?

Speaker: B:
Text: I didn’t play but one year in college.

Speaker: L:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: L:
Text: Because you were teaching.

Speaker: B:
Text: I didn’t go to college but one year, 'cause then I went welding.

Speaker: L:
Text: Okay, so you did three years of college and then your last year you just decided to do welding instead?

Speaker: B:
Text: Mhm.

Speaker: L:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: U:
Text: So then one year --

Speaker: B:
Text: I went to work.

Speaker: B:
Text: You know, in Virginia.

Speaker: L:
Text: In Virginia.

Speaker: L:
Text: So you became a welder.

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah.

Speaker: L:
Text: That must have been — was that, were there a lot of women doing welding?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah.

Speaker: B:
Text: A lot of them.

Speaker: L:
Text: And did they -- go ahead, sorry.

Speaker: B:
Text: They couldn’t get but just third-class welder.

Speaker: B:
Text: Men, you might weld better then a man, but the man could get a first-class welder job.

Speaker: B:
Text: But the womans couldn’t, she only got a third-class rating.

Speaker: B:
Text: But it was enough, you know, to help her family, for her to help her family, you know.

Speaker: L:
Text: Did you ever try to bring up the issue of being paid less than a man to your supervisors?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, a lot of them.

Speaker: B:
Text: It was a lot of women there, you know.

Speaker: B:
Text: They was higher educated then I was, they'd talk to ‘em.

Speaker: B:
Text: It didn’t matter.

Speaker: B:
Text: I only had one year of college when I went, but there were some that was higher then me couldn’t do anything.

Speaker: B:
Text: But I could weld just as good as some of the first-class welder men.

Speaker: B:
Text: I learned how to weld as soon as I went there and started trying to learn.

Speaker: B:
Text: I learned how to weld, it's something I like doing.

Speaker: L:
Text: Now, was it a welding school?

Speaker: B:
Text: They had a welding school that you could go to.

Speaker: L:
Text: And who taught you?

Speaker: L:
Text: So where did you go in Virginia?

Speaker: B:
Text: They had it right there on the -- you know, almost, you know, near where you worked.

Speaker: B:
Text: They had a building that they trained people.

Speaker: L:
Text: Now was this part of World War II in any way?

Speaker: B:
Text: What?

Speaker: L:
Text: Was this a part of the war effort?

Speaker: B:
Text: They paid you for what you done.

Speaker: B:
Text: It’s just that hiring you to do a job.

Speaker: B:
Text: It wasn’t a part of war.

Speaker: B:
Text: They just have a, they just hired you if you could do the job like they wanted it done.

Speaker: U1:
Text: That was during that time.

Speaker: U1:
Text: That was during World War II.

Speaker: B:
Text: We didn’t have no welding, you know.

Speaker: B:
Text: But the Shangri-la, Lake Champlain, those ships was the ones I worked with.

Speaker: B:
Text: You know, that been years ago.

Speaker: L:
Text: What kind of ships are those?

Speaker: B:
Text: Well, some were carrier and some was transports.

Speaker: B:
Text: They had different ships but mostly we worked on carriers and transports.

Speaker: L:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: L:
Text: So you were, you went, you did one year of college at A&M, and then you moved to Virginia to be a welder.

Speaker: L:
Text: But how did you learn about welding, this opportunity to get a job welding?

Speaker: B:
Text: My brother was in Georgia and he was telling me that the women could do the same thing.

Speaker: B:
Text: I taught school one year.

Speaker: B:
Text: But he was telling me about welding and I could get more money.

Speaker: B:
Text: So that’s why I went.

Speaker: B:
Text: But I couldn’t go nowhere but Virginia.

Speaker: B:
Text: Portsmouth.

Speaker: B:
Text: But Norfolk was the main headquarters.

Speaker: B:
Text: But I lived in Portsmouth because, you could, easy to go to the job from Portsmouth.

Speaker: B:
Text: You know, just go down the end of the street, and cut across and go to the lake.

Speaker: L:
Text: Was that scary for you to move so far away from your family?

Speaker: B:
Text: No, I didn’t think nothing about it.

Speaker: B:
Text: I just wanted to work.

Speaker: L:
Text: And so why did you stop being a welder?

Speaker: B:
Text: Why did I stop being a welder?

Speaker: B:
Text: What did I doing after that?

Speaker: B:
Text: Started working at Sunland Training Center, wasn't it?

Speaker: U1:
Text: Yeah, you got married and started a family in-between.

Speaker: U1:
Text: And then you went to work at Sunland.

Speaker: B:
Text: And then, you know, I started working at Sunland.

Speaker: B:
Text: Because Sunland Training Center was training children, and I loved that.

Speaker: B:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: L:
Text: So you were, when did you get married?

Speaker: L:
Text: How did you meet your husband?

Speaker: B:
Text: Oh, we were living in the same town, and he came out of service.

Speaker: L:
Text: In Virginia?

Speaker: B:
Text: No, we was back to Hawthorne.

Speaker: L:
Text: All right.

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, I met him, so when I decided to go back home, that’s when I thought, you know, I decided to go back home and marry him.

Speaker: B:
Text: So I be home.

Speaker: L:
Text: So did you decide to go back to Hawthorne in order to get married?

Speaker: B:
Text: Not exactly.

Speaker: B:
Text: You know.

Speaker: B:
Text: They was 'bout to catch up, we had done all the ship building mostly they were gone do.

Speaker: B:
Text: We worked a long many years there.

Speaker: U1:
Text: Our daddy died in '46 and you came back home after that.

Speaker: L:
Text: So your dad died in 1946 after the war ended?

Speaker: B:
Text: Mhm.

Speaker: U1:
Text: It was in September of — our Dad died in October.

Speaker: B:
Text: I’ve had a lot of sickness since then, you know, when you don’t keep up with something you can’t tell it like it is.

Speaker: B:
Text: But if you just remember it, you can tell that part you remember and the parts you just don’t remember, you just don’t bother with.

Speaker: B:
Text: Some, you just forget anyway.

Speaker: B:
Text: Cause it’s not necessary, you know.

Speaker: B:
Text: Not something that you had any problem with or anything.

Speaker: B:
Text: That part you had problem with, you remember it moreso than anything.

Speaker: L:
Text: That’s true.

Speaker: L:
Text: So what do you remember about that time?

Speaker: B:
Text: About, you know, it’s be -- it's a struggle is to how you have to do with the people that you working with, where you go, and, you know, how you take things.

Speaker: B:
Text: Cause see, we lived with a family of people but when you go to work, you don’t know where they gonna put you.

Speaker: B:
Text: And you got to know how to manage the people you're with, 'cause see , I was over a lot of people hadn’t been working with in years.

Speaker: B:

Speaker: B:

Text: And then how long was the, what was the church like?

Speaker: L:

Speaker: B:
Text: He could preach God’s word too and be happy people.

Speaker: B:
Text: People all in the choir happy.

Speaker: B:
Text: He could sing to them.

Speaker: B:
Text: You know, it’s good when you go to church when people seem to love the Lord and trying to work for the Lord.

Speaker: B:
Text: It means a lot to me.

Speaker: B:
Text: It means a lot.

Speaker: B:
Text: Cause Reverend Munn, he could sing, he could sing -- them people just shout all over him.

Speaker: B:
Text: It was just an enjoyment to see what was going on there.

Speaker: L:
Text: Did it take most of your day?

Speaker: L:
Text: Were you in the church for a lot of time?

Text: No, see, you just go there for the eleven o’clock service.

Speaker: B:
Text: If you wanted to go to for six o’clock service, you went there for that.

Speaker: B:
Text: If you go for the eleven o’clock service, fafter the eleven o’clock service, you go ahead and stay if you wanna stay.

Speaker: B:
Text: If you don't wanna go out no more that day.

Speaker: B:
Text: If you away from the church a long ways and had to walk.

Speaker: B:
Text: You don’t go back at night and have to walk in the night and come back home.

Speaker: L:
Text: So what did you all do?

Speaker: B:
Text: We stayed home a lot of time at night, so if we had a way to ride, we would stay for night service.

Text: How long was it when you started at eleven, when did you get out of y our church.

Speaker: B:
Text: And then about one-thirty, you out of church for the day.

Text: And then did you stay in town or did you go back home?

Speaker: B:

Text: We be driving, most of the time.

Speaker: B:
Text: Cause we was Baptist and we had a Methodist church that we could see from our house, but we weren’t Methodist.

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah.

Speaker: B:

Text: Wow.

Text: Sometime the house would be full of Blacks and sometime be full of Whites.

Speaker: B:
Text: They’d be friendly, they would be friendly now.

Speaker: B:
Text: No.

Speaker: B:
Text: Sometime, both sides have.

Text: What about during the Civil Rights Movement?

Text: Well, they didn’t pay no attention to that.

Speaker: B:
Text: I don’t know of any, you know, problems that way.

Speaker: B:
Text: You know, if they like, if one liked the other then they liked them; if they didn’t, they didn’t bother with them most of the time.

Text: Do you remember what you thought about Martin Luther King?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, but look, see, now that was a different thing.

Speaker: B:
Text: He was leading, you know, where somebody didn’t want him to lead.

Speaker: B:
Text: I think it’s what happened there.

Speaker: B:
Text: You know sometime you want to do one thing and somebody want you to do another.

Speaker: B:
Text: They want you to do what they want you to do.

Speaker: B:
Text: And a lot of time that bring on problems.

Speaker: B:
Text: But a lot of time, people don’t think about what you doing as long as you don’t bother them.

Speaker: B:
Text: People think nothing about it.

Text: So you never faced any kind of discrimination when you were living here?

Speaker: B:
Text: Unh-uh.

Speaker: L:
Text: Wow.

Text: Go to game, go to basketball games, and they were integrated, White and Black.

Speaker: B:
Text: You know, playing.

Text: Everybody out here planning on doing the same thing, picking up the same thing, and looking at the same thing.

Speaker: B:

Speaker: B:
Text: You wonder.

Speaker: U1:

Speaker: B:
Text: It won’t be, they won’t separate us, they ain't gone separate nobody.

Speaker: B:

Text: You know God, you know His ways.

Speaker: B:
Text: People don’t understand, you know, sometime we don’t understand things.

Speaker: B:
Text: And you know, God, He's for all, He done have -- He made them, He made us all.

Speaker: B:
Text: And I don’t think God would have made anybody like that evil, do all that for work.

Speaker: B:
Text: You just have to learn how to do things His way and that’s all.

Text: And they just liable to do anything, but you don’t want your child around somebody doing anything.

Speaker: B:

Speaker: B:

Speaker: B:

Speaker: B:

Speaker: B:
Text: But if you know and they're taught, it’s a different thing, it’s a different thing.

Speaker: B:

Speaker: B:

Speaker: B:
Text: So, it just cause trouble.

Speaker: B:
Text: And that’s the way it is.

Text: Don’t pick at them and don’t try to hurt them.

Speaker: B:
Text: They’re different, they’re just different.
